title: “IF YOUR BROTHER SINS AGAINST YOU…” — JESUS GAVE INSTRUCTIONS MOST CHRISTIANS SKIP
paragraphs: “IF YOUR BROTHER SINS AGAINST YOU…” — JESUS GAVE INSTRUCTIONS MOST CHRISTIANS SKIP

Before you expose their sin, tell your friends what happened, post about their betrayal, or decide they are dead to you… Jesus has something to say. And what He commanded in Matthew 18 may confront the way you have been handling the people who hurt you.
There is a conversation you have probably rehearsed a hundred times in your head.
You know exactly what they did.
You remember the words. The look on their face. The moment something inside you changed.
Maybe it was a friend you trusted with something you had never told anyone else.
Maybe it was someone in your church who smiled at you on Sunday, then spoke against you on Monday.
Maybe it was a brother or sister in Christ who knew your weaknesses and used them against you.
Or maybe it was someone you loved so deeply that you never imagined you would have to recover from what they did.
And now, whenever their name comes up, something happens inside your chest.
You tell yourself you have forgiven them.
You tell yourself you have moved on.
But you still remember.
You still replay the conversation.
You still imagine what you would say if you finally had the opportunity to tell everyone what really happened.
And perhaps the most painful part is that they seem perfectly fine while you are still carrying the damage.
So you talk to someone.
Then someone else.
You explain what happened. You defend yourself. You show the messages. You share the screenshots.
You want somebody to understand.
You want somebody to say, "You were right. They were wrong."
And sometimes you genuinely need help, protection, or wise counsel.
But sometimes, without realizing it, the search for understanding becomes an audience for our resentment.
The wound becomes a story.
The story becomes a reputation.
And before we have even spoken honestly to the person who hurt us, half the congregation knows what happened.
Then, somewhere in the middle of all that pain, Jesus speaks.
Not with a slogan.
Not with a motivational quotation about cutting people off.
Not with permission to pretend the offense never happened.
He gives instructions.
And the uncomfortable truth is that many of us have memorized the part of Christianity that tells us to forgive, while overlooking the part that tells us how to confront.
Listen carefully.
"Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother." — Matthew 18:15, KJV
Read those words again.
Not because they are complicated.
But because they are painfully clear.
"If thy brother shall trespass against thee..."
Jesus begins by acknowledging something many wounded Christians need to hear.
Your brother can actually sin against you.
A fellow believer can betray your trust.
A church member can lie.
A ministry leader can mistreat someone.
Someone who knows Scripture can still behave in a way that contradicts it.
Jesus does not require you to rename wrongdoing as a misunderstanding just to keep the peace.
He does not say the wound is imaginary.
He does not command you to smile while pretending that nothing happened.
He calls the offense what it is.
Sin.
But then He gives a command that cuts directly across our instincts.
"Go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone."
Go.
Not immediately to the congregation.
Not first to the group chat.
Not straight to Facebook.
Go to the person.
And here is where we need to understand the original language.
In the Greek text of Matthew 18:15, Jesus says:
ὕπαγε ἔλεγξον αὐτὸν μεταξὺ σοῦ καὶ αὐτοῦ μόνου
Hypage elenxon auton metaxy sou kai autou monou.
A faithful rendering is:
"Go, show him his fault between you and him alone."
The word ἔλεγξον (elenxon) comes from a verb meaning to expose, reprove, or bring a fault to light.
It does not mean to humiliate someone publicly for emotional satisfaction.
It is a call to confront wrongdoing truthfully.
And notice the expression μεταξὺ σοῦ καὶ αὐτοῦ μόνου — "between you and him alone."
Jesus deliberately describes a private encounter.
Why?
Because the goal is not to win an audience.
The goal is to gain a brother.
That is the part many of us have missed.
We approach conflict wanting vindication.
Jesus teaches us to pursue restoration.
We want the other person to admit we were right.
Jesus wants truth to produce repentance and, where possible, reconciliation.
We want to prove how badly someone failed us.
Jesus wants sin confronted without unnecessarily destroying the person who committed it.
And no, that does not mean every situation is safe for a private meeting.

If someone has abused, threatened, assaulted, coerced, or endangered you, you are not required to meet that person alone. Seek protection, involve appropriate authorities, and obtain trustworthy help. Criminal conduct should not be concealed under the language of church reconciliation. Matthew 18 is not a command to place yourself or others in danger.
But for ordinary interpersonal offenses where a private conversation is appropriate and safe, the instruction is astonishingly practical.
Before you make their failure public, give truth an opportunity to work privately.
Before you recruit people to your side, consider whether you have genuinely attempted to reach their conscience.
Before you assume they will never listen, ask whether you have actually spoken to them.
That last question may hurt.
Because sometimes we have had ten conversations about someone without having one honest conversation with them.
And sometimes we call it seeking prayer when, deep down, we are hoping others will share our anger.
There is a difference between seeking wise counsel and spreading damaging information unnecessarily.
There is a difference between reporting serious misconduct and broadcasting a personal offense.
There is a difference between telling the truth for protection and telling the truth as a weapon.
Truth can be spoken with sinful motives.
And being genuinely wounded does not make every response to that wound righteous.
I know.
That is difficult to receive when you are the one who was hurt.
Because pain has a way of convincing us that whatever we do next must be justified.
But Jesus loves us too much to let another person's sin become permission for our own.
And then comes one of the most beautiful phrases in the entire passage.
"If he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother."
The Greek reads:
ἐκέρδησας τὸν ἀδελφόν σου
Ekerdēsas ton adelphon sou.
"You have gained your brother."
The verb ἐκέρδησας (ekerdēsas) carries the sense of gaining or winning.
Think about that.
Jesus does not say, "You have won the argument."
He does not say, "You have defeated your enemy."
He says you have gained your brother.
What a different vision of victory.
Imagine two believers sitting across from one another.
One is trembling because speaking honestly is difficult.
The other is uncomfortable because the truth is exposing something they would rather deny.
There is no audience.
No applause.
No public humiliation.
Just truth, humility, and the possibility of repentance.
Then perhaps the offender says words that seemed impossible only yesterday.
"I was wrong."
"I should never have said that."
"I hurt you."
"Will you forgive me?"
And suddenly, what could have become years of bitterness begins moving toward healing.
Not because the sin was small.
Not because the wound was imaginary.
But because someone obeyed Jesus when retaliation would have been easier.
This is what restoration can look like.
Not always.
Not automatically.
But sometimes.
And those moments matter.
Because there are friendships that might still exist if someone had spoken privately before speaking publicly.
There are families that might have avoided years of unnecessary division.
There are churches where conflicts might have been addressed before rumors multiplied.
Not every relationship can or should be restored to its previous level of closeness. Trust may require time, accountability, changed behavior, and appropriate boundaries.
But where genuine repentance and safe reconciliation are possible, Christians should not treat restoration as an embarrassing defeat.
It is something worth pursuing.
Now perhaps you are thinking:
"But what if I go to them and they refuse to listen?"
Jesus anticipated that.
"But if he will not hear thee, then take with thee one or two more, that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established." — Matthew 18:16, KJV
Notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not say, "If they refuse, tell everybody."
He introduces another measured step.
Bring one or two others.
Why?
Not to assemble a cheering section.
Not to intimidate the offender.
Not to make the confrontation feel like an ambush.
The witnesses help establish what is said, clarify the facts, and support a just and accountable process.
Jesus echoes the principle found in Deuteronomy 19:15, where matters are established through adequate testimony.
In other words, righteousness requires more than strong feelings.
It requires truth.
It requires fairness.
It requires listening.
It requires the humility to recognize that even when we have been hurt, our understanding of every detail may not be complete.
That is hard to admit.
Especially when the pain feels undeniable.
But Scripture does not teach that emotional certainty is the same as complete knowledge.
Proverbs 18:17 says:
"He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him."
The first account may sound convincing until further examination.
That does not mean every accusation is false.
It means justice must be careful.
And Christians, of all people, should understand why.
We serve a Savior who was falsely accused.
A Savior whose enemies twisted His words.
A Savior who stood before people determined to condemn Him.
We should never be careless with another person's reputation.
Even when confrontation is necessary.
Even when wrongdoing is real.
Then Jesus continues.
"And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church..." — Matthew 18:17, KJV
Only now does the process reach the wider church community.
Not as entertainment.
Not as an invitation to gossip.
Not as a social media spectacle.
But as a serious matter requiring responsible spiritual oversight and accountability.
And if the offender refuses even the church's correction, Jesus describes a change in how that person is to be regarded.
This is sobering.
Church discipline is not supposed to be a performance of superiority. It is a serious response to persistent, unrepentant sin, carried out with justice, humility, and a desire for repentance.
The apostle Paul expresses that restorative concern in Galatians 6:1:
"Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted."
Restore.
In meekness.
While remembering your own vulnerability.
That is not the language of a spiritual mob.
That is the language of a family that understands both the seriousness of sin and the necessity of grace.
And this is where the passage becomes even more uncomfortable.
Because some of us are reading this while thinking about the person who wronged us.
But what if the Holy Spirit is also showing us how we have wronged someone else?
What if we have been the one who refused correction?
What if someone tried to speak to us privately, and we became defensive?
What if they told us we had hurt them, and instead of listening, we immediately began explaining why their feelings were unreasonable?
What if we apologized with words that sounded like repentance but actually shifted the blame?
"I'm sorry you felt that way."
"I'm sorry you misunderstood."
"I'm sorry, but you made me angry."
What if the hardest sentence for us to say is simply:
"I sinned against you, and I was wrong."
There is a particular kind of pride that hides behind religious language.
It quotes verses.
It serves in ministry.
It knows how to pray in public.
But it cannot bear to be corrected in private.
And Scripture confronts that pride.
"He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy." — Proverbs 28:13, KJV
Confession without forsaking sin is incomplete.
An apology without genuine change may be nothing more than an attempt to end an uncomfortable conversation.
And repentance is more than feeling bad because someone discovered what we did.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) is commonly translated "repentance." It speaks of a change of mind or heart that, in biblical teaching, is expressed through a changed direction of life.
Real repentance does not merely ask, "How can I make this problem disappear?"
It asks, "How have I sinned before God, and what must change?"
Sometimes repentance includes restitution.
Sometimes it requires admitting the truth to people we misled.
Sometimes it means accepting consequences.
Sometimes it means understanding that forgiveness does not automatically restore the trust we damaged.
And sometimes it means giving the person we hurt the time and space they need.
Because grace is not permission to escape accountability.
Grace teaches us to turn away from ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 says that the grace of God teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live soberly, righteously, and godly.
That is transforming grace.
Not grace that protects our pride.
Grace that changes us.
But now we must look at what happens immediately after Jesus gives these instructions.
Because Matthew 18 does not end with confrontation.
Peter approaches Jesus with a question that sounds very familiar to anyone who has ever grown tired of forgiving.
"Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?" — Matthew 18:21, KJV
You can almost hear the exhaustion.
How many times, Lord?
How many times do I have to deal with this?
How many times must I release my desire for revenge?
How many times can somebody hurt me before I am finally allowed to stop forgiving?
Peter suggests seven times.
That probably sounded generous.
But Jesus responds:
"I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven." — Matthew 18:22, KJV
Jesus is not giving Peter a literal quota of 490 offenses.
He is overturning the idea that forgiveness should be managed with a scorecard.
Then He tells the parable of the unforgiving servant.
A man owes his king an enormous debt.
He cannot pay.
Judgment is approaching.
He begs for mercy.
And the king, moved with compassion, releases him and forgives the debt.
Imagine the relief.
Imagine walking out of that room knowing the burden you could never repay has been lifted.
But then the forgiven servant finds another servant who owes him a much smaller amount.
He grabs him.
Demands payment.
Refuses mercy.
The man who had just received extraordinary forgiveness becomes merciless toward someone else.
And Jesus exposes the contradiction.
How can a person receive such great mercy and then refuse to extend mercy?
This is where the story stops being about the person who offended you.
And starts being about your heart before God.
Because the Gospel begins with a debt we could never pay.
Not a financial debt.
A moral and spiritual debt created by our sin.
We have not merely been misunderstood.
We have sinned against a holy God.
We have loved things more than Him.
We have spoken words we should never have spoken.
We have concealed motives.
We have entertained bitterness.
We have justified pride.
We have failed to love our neighbors as ourselves.
And the frightening truth is that no amount of religious activity can erase our guilt.
We cannot purchase forgiveness.
We cannot earn salvation through good behavior.
We cannot make ourselves righteous by comparing our sins with somebody else's.
"For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God." — Romans 3:23, KJV
All.
The person who hurt you.
And you.
The person who betrayed your trust.
And you.
The person whose sin became public.
And the person whose sin remained hidden.
All of us need mercy.
And then comes Jesus Christ.
The sinless Son of God.
The One who never lied.
Never betrayed.
Never acted from selfish pride.
Never sinned against His Father.
Yet He willingly gave Himself for sinners.
At the cross, Jesus did not pretend sin was harmless.
He bore its judgment.
He did not dismiss evil as insignificant.
He gave His life to redeem people from it.
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." — Romans 5:8, KJV
While we were still sinners.
Not after we repaired ourselves.
Not after we became worthy.
Not after we finally learned how to behave.
Christ died for us while we were guilty.
And through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are proclaimed to everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith.
This is why Christian forgiveness is so different from pretending nothing happened.
God's forgiveness is not denial.
It is mercy grounded in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And when we understand how much mercy we have received, it begins to change how we treat those who sin against us.
Not by making evil acceptable.
Not by removing appropriate consequences.
Not by requiring victims to remain in harmful situations.
But by loosening the grip of vengeance on our hearts.
Romans 12:19 reminds believers not to avenge themselves, but to leave vengeance to God.
And Ephesians 4:32 says:
"And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you."
For Christ's sake.
There it is.
The center of everything.
We do not forgive because the offense was insignificant.
We forgive because Christ has shown us mercy beyond anything we could earn.
And we do not confront because we enjoy exposing people.
We confront because truth matters, sin destroys, and love must sometimes say difficult things.
Jesus Himself holds grace and truth together.
John 1:14 describes Him as "full of grace and truth."
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Both.
And this is the balance so many Christians desperately need.
Some people use forgiveness to avoid necessary confrontation.
They remain silent while resentment grows.
They say, "I forgive you," but never address patterns that continue damaging the relationship.
Others use confrontation as an excuse to punish.
They expose, embarrass, and condemn, then call it biblical accountability.
But Jesus calls us to something better.
Truth without cruelty.
Mercy without denial.
Courage without arrogance.
Forgiveness without pretending that repentance, accountability, and trust are meaningless.
And perhaps the most searching question is this:
Do you actually want your brother or sister restored, or do you only want them exposed?
Think carefully before answering.
Because sometimes we become so attached to being the injured person that the possibility of reconciliation almost feels threatening.
We have told the story so many times.
We have received sympathy.
We have built our understanding of the relationship around what they did.
And now, if they genuinely repent, we may have to release the version of the story in which they are only the villain and we are only the victim.
That does not mean the harm disappears.
It does not mean reconciliation is always possible.
It does not mean trust should be restored without evidence of change.
But it does mean we must examine whether bitterness has become part of our identity.
Hebrews 12:15 warns believers about a root of bitterness that can spring up and trouble many.
Notice that bitterness rarely remains private.
It spreads.
It influences how we interpret people.
It changes how we speak.
It teaches us to expect betrayal everywhere.
And sometimes it makes us suspicious of people who never harmed us.
One wound begins shaping an entire life.
Perhaps that is where you are today.
You still attend church.
You still listen to sermons.
You still post Scripture.
You still tell people that God is good.
But there is a name you cannot hear without anger rising inside you.
And you are tired.
Tired of remembering.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of carrying a conversation that never happened.
You may not be ready to speak to that person today.
You may need counsel.
You may need distance.
You may need protection.
You may need to grieve what was lost.
But you can begin by bringing the truth of your heart before Jesus.
Not the polished version.
The real one.
"Lord, I am angry."
"Lord, I feel betrayed."
"Lord, I want them to understand what they did."
"Lord, I don't know how to forgive."
"Lord, I am afraid that if I let go of this bitterness, nobody will ever acknowledge what happened."
God is not confused by your pain.
Psalm 62:8 invites His people to pour out their hearts before Him.
You do not have to manufacture an emotion you do not feel.
But you can surrender your desire for revenge.
You can ask God for wisdom.
You can refuse to turn your wound into a weapon.
You can choose to pursue truth in a way that honors Christ.
And if the person who hurt you never repents?
That is a painful possibility.
Matthew 18 itself recognizes that some people refuse correction.
You cannot force repentance.
You cannot make another person acknowledge what they did.
You cannot single-handedly restore a relationship that requires honesty and willingness from both sides.
Romans 12:18 says:
"If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men."
Those words matter.
"If it be possible."
"As much as lieth in you."
Scripture recognizes that peace is not always achievable through one person's efforts.
You are responsible for your obedience.
You are not responsible for controlling another person's heart.
And sometimes the most faithful response is to forgive while maintaining necessary boundaries, seeking appropriate accountability, and entrusting the unresolved matter to God.
But there is another side of this message.
Maybe you are not the wounded person in the story.
Maybe you are the one who caused the wound.
Maybe somebody tried to tell you.
Maybe they said, "What you did hurt me."
And you dismissed them.
Maybe you accused them of being too sensitive.
Maybe you brought up their past mistakes to avoid discussing your own.
Maybe you recruited friends to defend you.
Maybe you have spent years telling your version of events because you are terrified of what admitting the truth might cost.
Listen.
There is still mercy in Christ for repentant sinners.
You do not have to keep defending what God is calling you to confess.
You do not have to spend the rest of your life protecting a false image of yourself.
You can humble yourself.
You can tell the truth.
You can apologize without excuses.
You can make restitution where appropriate.
You can accept accountability.
And you can ask Jesus to transform the heart that produced the sin.
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — 1 John 1:9, KJV
What a promise.
Not that confession removes every earthly consequence.
Not that every broken relationship will immediately be restored.
But that God is faithful to forgive and cleanse those who come to Him according to His promise.
This is the beauty of the Gospel.
It does not merely tell wounded people to become stronger.
It offers them a Savior.
It does not merely tell guilty people to become better.
It offers them forgiveness and a new life through Jesus Christ.
It does not merely expose sin.
It announces redemption.
And that brings us to something we cannot afford to miss.
The same chapter that teaches us how to confront a sinning brother also reveals the heart of a Father who cares for the wandering.
In Matthew 18:12–14, Jesus speaks of a shepherd who seeks a sheep that has gone astray.
The surrounding context reminds us that God's concern is not merely procedural correctness.
He cares about people.
About those who wander.
About those who need to be brought back.
About those who must be protected.
About those whose souls are in danger.
That does not erase the need for discernment or accountability.
It reveals why those things matter.
Biblical correction should never become an excuse to enjoy someone's downfall.
And biblical compassion should never become an excuse to ignore serious sin.
The church belongs to Jesus.
Its purpose is not to protect appearances at the expense of truth.
Its calling is to honor Christ through holiness, justice, mercy, love, and faithfulness.
Imagine what would change if believers began taking Matthew 18 seriously.
Imagine Christians who refused to spread rumors simply because they were angry.
Imagine leaders who listened carefully rather than automatically defending their friends.
Imagine people who admitted wrongdoing without blaming those they hurt.
Imagine churches that protected vulnerable people while pursuing fair and responsible accountability.
Imagine friendships where difficult conversations happened before resentment became hatred.
Imagine families where the words "I was wrong" were no longer treated as humiliation.
Imagine a community where grace was not confused with secrecy and truth was not confused with cruelty.
Would every relationship be repaired?
No.
Would every offender repent?
No.
Would every wound disappear?
No.
But Christ would be honored through obedience.
And that matters more than winning an argument.
Perhaps you are reading this with tears in your eyes because someone came to mind.
Perhaps it is a person you need to approach.
Perhaps it is someone you need to forgive.
Perhaps it is someone you need to stop speaking against.
Perhaps it is someone you owe a genuine apology.
Or perhaps you need to seek help because what happened was too serious to handle alone.
Whatever your situation, do not turn this passage into another weapon against someone else.
Let it examine your own heart first.
Ask yourself:
Have I pursued truth or merely sympathy?
Have I sought restoration or retaliation?
Have I spoken with humility?
Have I listened when corrected?
Have I confused forgiveness with the absence of boundaries?
Have I allowed bitterness to become a permanent residence in my heart?
And most importantly:
Am I willing to obey Jesus even when His instructions challenge what I feel entitled to do?
Because following Christ is not merely agreeing with His words when they comfort us.
It is submitting to His authority when they confront us.
Jesus said in Luke 6:46:
"And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?"
That question should stop us.
We cannot claim that Jesus is Lord while treating His commands as optional whenever obedience becomes inconvenient.
But remember this too.
Our obedience does not purchase God's love.
We obey because He first loved us.
We pursue holiness because His grace has reached us.
We forgive because we have been forgiven.
We confront sin because Christ is worthy of truth.
We pursue reconciliation where possible because Jesus has reconciled sinners to God through His cross.
And when we fail, we return to Him in repentance.
Again.
And again.
Not because grace is cheap.
But because Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
That is why the theme of Gospel Warrior is more than a memorable phrase.
Think of Peter.
He denied Jesus three times.
Not privately in the safety of his own thoughts.
Openly.
Under pressure.
He denied knowing the Lord he had promised never to abandon.
Then the rooster crowed.
And Peter wept bitterly.
Imagine the shame.
The memory of his own voice.
The knowledge that he had failed the One who loved him.
But Peter's failure was not the final chapter.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter and, in John 21, lovingly recommissioned him to care for His sheep.
Peter was not restored because denial was harmless.
He was restored by the grace of the risen Christ.
The same Peter who once denied his Lord later boldly proclaimed Him.
That is not a story about human perfection.
It is a testimony to the power of Jesus.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to know that their worst chapter does not have to become their final chapter.
If you are the one who sinned, repent and come to Christ.
If you are the one who was wounded, bring your pain to Christ.
If you are caught in bitterness, ask Christ to free your heart.
If you are afraid to tell the truth, ask Christ for courage.
If you have been hiding behind a religious appearance, stop running from the Savior who already knows the truth.
Jesus is not asking you to save yourself.
He is calling you to follow Him.
And that changes everything.
Before you leave this article, I want to ask you something personal.
Not for appearances.
Not to make yourself look spiritual.
But because there may be another believer reading the comments who thinks they are the only one struggling.
If you are exhausted from carrying a wound, you can comment, "Pray for me."
If you recognize that you have been avoiding a necessary apology, you can comment, "Lord, humble my heart."
If this message has challenged how you handle conflict, you can comment, "Teach me to obey, Jesus."
And if you have experienced genuine restoration through repentance and forgiveness, consider sharing a brief testimony. Your experience may encourage someone who has almost given up hope.
You do not have to reveal names, private details, or traumatic experiences publicly. God knows the prayers you cannot safely put into a comment.
And please, do not let this message stop with you.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be one angry conversation away from destroying a relationship that could still be repaired.
Someone may be carrying resentment that has quietly consumed years of their life.
Someone may be using Christian language to avoid admitting wrongdoing.
Someone may desperately need to hear that forgiveness is possible without surrendering safety or accountability.
Because a single article can challenge a heart.
But growing as a disciple requires continuing in the Word.
And that is why we are building something deeper than a collection of inspirational posts.
Our desire is to make biblical nourishment accessible, to help people understand Scripture in context, to encourage genuine repentance, and to point wounded and wandering hearts toward the Savior.
But producing, maintaining, and expanding this ministry takes ongoing support.
Not because you can purchase God's favor.
And certainly not because paying a ministry is a requirement for glorifying God.
You glorify God by trusting and obeying Jesus Christ, and one meaningful way you may choose to express that devotion is by generously supporting faithful Gospel ministry.
In Philippians 4:15–17, Paul acknowledges the generosity of believers who supported his ministry, describing their partnership as fruit credited to their account.
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
That last phrase matters.
Not grudgingly.
Not under compulsion.
Christian generosity should come from a willing heart.
Think about the person scrolling through Facebook late at night.
The believer who feels ashamed after falling into sin again.
The husband and wife who have stopped speaking.
The young person who is questioning whether God still cares.
The wounded Christian who has nearly abandoned church altogether.
The person who has never understood the Gospel clearly.
We cannot know in advance who will encounter a message or how God may use it.
But we can faithfully continue sowing the seed of His Word.
These items are simply expressions of appreciation. They are not spiritual rewards, and the discount is not a substitute for the eternal treasure found in Christ.
It is the opportunity to participate in making the message of Jesus Christ more widely known.
Pray for this ministry.
Sometimes a simple act of sharing brings Scripture to a person who might never have searched for it.
Your participation matters, even when you cannot contribute financially.
Because the mission has never been to build an audience around a personality.
It is to point people toward Jesus Christ.
And that brings us back to the words with which we began.
"If thy brother shall trespass against thee..."
Maybe the person who came to mind at the beginning of this article is still on your heart.
Maybe you now understand that you need to have a difficult conversation.
Maybe you need to repent before expecting someone else to repent.
Maybe you need to stop repeating a story that no longer needs another audience.
Maybe you need to tell a trusted leader about serious wrongdoing that must not remain hidden.
Maybe you need to forgive while accepting that reconciliation is not presently safe or possible.
Or maybe, for the first time in a long time, you need to stop looking at everybody else's sin and bring your own heart before the cross.
Whatever the next faithful step looks like, take it with Jesus.
Not with pride.
Not with revenge.
Not with fear disguised as wisdom.
With truth.
With humility.
With courage.
With grace.
Because the goal is not simply to have the last word.
The goal is to honor the One who gave His life to reconcile sinners to God.

And one day, when the arguments are over, when the posts have disappeared, when the people who applauded our anger have moved on, and when every hidden motive stands before the Lord, what will matter is not how successfully we defended our pride.
What will matter is whether we belonged to Jesus and followed Him in faith.
So before you expose your brother's sin, remember Matthew 18.
Before you excuse your own sin, remember the cross.
Before you surrender to bitterness, remember the mercy you have received.
And before you decide that a broken story can never be redeemed, remember the empty tomb.
The wound may explain why you are hurting, but it does not have to become the author of who you are becoming. Jesus can write the next chapter.
